name: Napping / NSDR / yoga nidra

lead: These are brief rest practices: daytime naps, and guided relaxation known as yoga nidra or non-sleep deep rest (NSDR). People use them to make up for short nights and lower stress, aiming for a fresher, less drawn face.

Naps restore alertness through short sleep, and studies report benefits for alertness and memory. Yoga nidra is a guided body-awareness meditation done lying down, described as between waking and sleeping, with small studies on relaxation. NSDR is a newer label for similar guided-rest protocols. None of the research looks at appearance.

paras: People nap for a short period in the early afternoon, or lie down with a recorded yoga nidra or NSDR session of around 10 to 30 minutes. They are often used after a poor night or between training and work. Effects on energy are typically felt right after.
Long naps can cause grogginess, and habitual long napping is linked with health risks in observational data. Naps late in the day can make night sleep harder.

social.title: Polyphasic sleep takes napping to the extreme

angle.text: Short naps and guided deep-rest sessions restore energy and lower stress, which users link to a fresher, less tired-looking face. Naps have been studied for alertness and memory, and yoga nidra has small studies on relaxation; appearance has not been studied.

lead: Napping, non-sleep deep rest (NSDR) and yoga nidra are short rest practices used to recover energy, reduce stress and make up for lost sleep. A nap is a short daytime sleep; yoga nidra is a guided, lying-down meditation often described as a state between waking and sleeping; NSDR is a newer label for similar guided-rest protocols.[1][2] In looksmaxxing communities they are used as part of a recovery routine meant to support how a person looks: more rested eyes and skin, better training recovery and more alertness and energy.[3][4]

Forum authors describe naps as an overlooked recovery tool, arguing that short midday sleep supports alertness, memory and training recovery, and some tie rest to aesthetics through a fresher, less tired appearance.[3] Athletic-performance research gives a related picture: a 2021 narrative review examined how daytime napping affects athletic performance.[5]
Research on naps reports benefits for alertness and memory, and early trials of yoga nidra report effects on sleep, stress and mood in small groups.[1][2][6][7]
infobox: Micro 2-5 min, power 10-30 min, full cycle about 90 min[1]

paras: Naps are categorised by duration, such as micro naps of a few minutes, power naps of 10-30 minutes and full-cycle naps of about 90 minutes.[1] Wikipedia reports that early afternoon is when sleepiness typically peaks and describes 20-30 minutes as a common recommendation for adults.[1] A NASA study is reported to show a 26-minute nap improved alertness by 54% and performance by 34% in pilots.[1]

Sleep inertia, the grogginess after waking, is more likely after longer naps that reach slow-wave sleep and rarely lasts beyond 30 minutes in people who are not sleep-deprived.[1] A 2016 meta-analysis linked habitual naps over an hour with higher cardiovascular and metabolic risk, with no causal link established, while naps up to 40 minutes showed no such association.[1] Sleep in general aids memory consolidation.[8]

Yoga nidra's modern form draws on Western relaxation methods; Satyananda Saraswati popularised a structured method in 1976, and Richard Miller developed iRest for soldiers with PTSD.[2] Claimed benefits include reduced anxiety and better sleep; a small trial of 45 male athletes found improved sleep latency and efficiency versus progressive muscle relaxation.[2]
NSDR is a newer name for similar guided-rest protocols and is not covered in Wikipedia's yoga nidra article.[2]

One looksmax.org thread presents the power nap as a forgotten part of recovery, describing short naps as improving reaction time, attention and memory consolidation, and warning that long naps can leave users groggy.[3] Replies in the thread mention sleeping for hours when attempting a nap and using phone alarms to limit it.[3] A separate thread discusses social perceptions of men napping.[9]

Nap research includes the NASA pilot study and the 2016 meta-analysis.[1] A 2021 narrative review examined daytime napping and athletic performance.[5] A Zurich crossover study in 70 healthy women found that a hypnotic suggestion to sleep deeper, played before a 90-minute nap, increased slow-wave sleep by 81 percent.[10]

Yoga nidra trials include a randomized sleep-lab feasibility study in 22 adults with self-reported insomnia,[11] a randomized trial in chronic insomnia,[12] and trials on stress and self-esteem in university students[6] and on anxiety and insomnia in COVID-19 frontline health workers.[7] No studies were found on NSDR as a named protocol.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org naps and rest appear within sleep-and-recovery discussions as a way to support performance and appearance.[3]
